warmup.text: Today's sentence has a clause tucked inside two commas. Tap it to see why. Then write: what is the most interesting difference between your two novels?

words.text: Edit two passages for spelling and mark every fix. Build words from their roots, then check your draft's sentence openers. Four new pairs are waiting in the game.

reading.text: Reread to test your claim against the books. Then finish your draft: your second category, your real-voice paragraph, and your closing. Read all five paragraphs out loud. The Read Like a Writer box helps you start the source paragraph.

assignment.text: Today is the revise day. Check your essay against the Revision Checklist, line by line. Fix what it finds, then paste the revised essay and write one change you made at the top.

readnow.text: No new chapter today. Finish your draft, then revise it with the checklist.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you work. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Testing a claim against the books makes it stronger, or shows you where to change it.
how.use: You will use it in draft question 3.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Fixing one kind of mistake at a time catches more of them.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on.
how.why: Thinking first gives you something to watch for.

do: Edit both passages in the box.
Mark each fix in [brackets].
how.why: This is your Show What You Know for spelling this week.

do: Revise one sentence in your draft with a root word, in your reading journal.
Type each word, then tap Check My Work.
how.why: A precise word is often a root word.

do: Revise one sentence opener in your reading journal.
Type the joining word in each sentence.
Tap Check My Work.
how.why: Joining words hold the two sides of a comparison together.

do: Read the How to Write box.
Write paragraphs 3 and 4 in the first box and your closing in the second.
Read all five out loud, then answer question 3.
how.why: Finishing the draft first gives you something whole to revise.

do: Read the Revision Checklist.
Revise all five paragraphs.
Paste the revised essay, with one change noted at the top.
how.why: A checklist catches what your eyes skip.

glossary.meaning: a word or phrase that joins ideas, like however or in contrast

manuscript: Think of a book written before printing presses.
fortitude: Strength that holds when things are hard.
Both: It shows two things are alike.
It goes before the two names.
Whereas: It sets up a contrast at the start.
It means while on the other hand.
Like: It shows a similarity, before a name.
however: A contrast word set off by commas.

game.title: Two Books, One Root
game.sub: This week's word game · 4 pairs today
game.look: Five novels and one more book on the shelf: You. Two words with the same root are a pair. Each pair you find ties two worlds together with a gold thread.

do: Tap a card to turn it over.
Tap a second card.
Same root? The pair stays up. Different roots? They turn back over.
how.why: A root is the same in every book. Spotting it lets you read a word you have never seen.

game.miss: Look for the same few letters inside both words.
game.doneLine: Come back next lesson for four new pairs.

pairs.why: Jack's hair falls in a yellow scribble in Chapter 1; a scribe is someone who writes things down, like you this week.
An audience hears a speech, like the Observers hearing James Otis; audible means loud enough to hear, like your read-aloud.
A chronometer keeps exact time at sea; a chronicle tells events in time order, like a year of reading.
Valuable means worth a lot; to evaluate is to decide what something is worth, like the evidence in your essay.

virtue.name: wisdom
virtue.moment: Praiseworthy powders the black sow with coal dust, so the thief gives himself away by never touching her (By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 2).
virtue.line: In one sentence: why did you put the slider there?
virtue.take: I'd put it near the top. Praiseworthy knew a guilty man would be afraid of a squeal, so he planned for what the thief would do, not just what the pig would do.

art.title: The Ship Mount Vernon of Salem
art.alt: A painting of a large three-masted sailing ship with full sails on a calm gray sea, puffs of cannon smoke near its side, and other ships far behind.
art.look: Michele Felice Corné painted the Salem ship Mount Vernon in 1799, the year he sailed on her to America. Here she fights off French privateers near Gibraltar. Nat Bowditch sailed from Salem on trading ships like this in those same years.
